meta_description: Class 7.1: Boolean Logic 101: True/False Legal Gates. Bridging static legal prose and active software runtimes by replacing ambiguous 'and/or' loopholes with strict Boolean true/false evaluation gates (==), Hats Protocol role trees, and Ricardian contracts.
hero_subtitle_html: Bridging static legal prose and active software runtimes by replacing ambiguous "and/or" loopholes with strict Boolean true/false evaluation gates (==), Hats Protocol role trees, and Ricardian contracts.
overview_html: Explores why the static paper medium holds back legal reasoning and how shifting to a computational calculus mindset turns a legal performance into an automated software runtime. Demonstrates why ambiguous "and/or" prose collapses inside Boolean true/false evaluation gates (==), how single equals (=) right-to-left variable assignment differs from double equals (==) comparison, and how Hats Protocol role trees and Ian Grigg's Ricardian contracts chain modular legal agreements together.
hub_card_summary_html: Bridging static legal contracts and active software runtimes with binary true/false legal gates, eliminating the "and/or" ambiguity trap, and building modular Hats Protocol chains.

socratic_companion.description_html: Explore the recorded Thursday, Nov 12, 2026 cohort Socratic discussion and 5 explainer clips for Class 7.1.

questions.prompt: According to Class 7.1, what happens when a static legal contract transitions into an active software runtime?

options.A: It transforms from passive paper into an executing performance — a living set of instructions waiting to trigger an action.
options.B: It remains a frozen PDF stored in a filing cabinet.
options.C: It requires a human judge to manually read every line before any payment can clear.

questions.prompt: How does Class 7.1 define the core function of Boolean logic gates in legal engineering?

options.A: Translating nuanced legal conditions and thresholds into absolute binary true or false gates that strictly control the flow of software execution.
options.B: Allowing contracts to remain intentionally vague so parties can negotiate later.
options.C: Replacing all numbers in a contract with poetic metaphors.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of the conditional translation process described in Class 7.1?

options.A: First isolate the specific legal obligation, second define it as a Boolean primitive (true or false), and third place it into an if/else statement.
options.B: Print the contract, sign it in ink, and mail it to a courthouse.
options.C: Delete all conditions, merge all clauses, and remove every variable.

questions.prompt: In Class 7.1's short-term rental smart-lock example, how does the if/else statement execute?

options.A: If the rent payment is received, release the digital key; else, keep the door locked.
options.B: Unlock the door regardless of whether rent was paid.
options.C: Send a paper eviction notice six months after checkout.

questions.prompt: Why does the traditional lawyer phrase 'and/or' cause a deterministic software runtime to fail in Class 7.1?

options.A: Because code cannot interpret a 'maybe' — if a legal condition is not strictly true or strictly false, the Boolean logic outright fails.
options.B: Because computers cannot read the slash character.
options.C: Because 'and/or' is only valid in criminal statutes.

questions.prompt: What metaphor does Class 7.1 use in Section 1 to contrast a dead piece of paper with an active runtime contract?

options.A: A composer's sheet music — designing the system beforehand, hitting play, and watching the stage performance execute.
options.B: A brick wall that never moves.
options.C: A painting hanging in a museum.

questions.prompt: What industry habit does Class 7.1 call 'static fixation'?

options.A: Viewing information as permanently frozen in a spreadsheet grid cell or on a physical page rather than as an active script.
options.B: Writing modular smart contracts on Ethereum.
options.C: Using double equals signs to evaluate conditions.

questions.prompt: How does Class 7.1's 'active canvas' decouple a computational contract?

options.A: It strictly decouples the passive assets (your data) from the active machinery (the actual instructions).
options.B: It combines all instructions and data into a single unindexed image.
options.C: It removes all variables from the runtime.

questions.prompt: Why do lawyers traditionally treat vagueness like 'and/or' as a feature rather than a bug in natural language drafting?

options.A: Because in human prose it leaves room for negotiation and gives clients wiggle room down the line.
options.B: Because it makes computer code compile faster.
options.C: Because it automatically enforces digital smart locks.

questions.prompt: What computer science mechanism does Class 7.1 compare to 'putting square pegs only into square holes'?

options.A: Data typing domains that strictly validate data to prevent errors at runtime.
options.B: Unstructured free-text footnotes.
options.C: Verbal handshake agreements.

questions.prompt: According to Section 4 of Class 7.1, what is the real friction lawyers face when adapting to a programming environment?

options.A: Not overarching logical reasoning, but micro-mechanics — specific syntax and grammatical hurdles like typing domains and the word 'equals'.
options.B: An inability to understand rules or obligations.
options.C: A lack of vocabulary in English.

questions.prompt: In Computational Legalese, what does a single equals sign (`=`) actually mean?

options.A: An active assignment instruction: take the value on the right (e.g., 10) and assign it into the variable bucket on the left (e.g., x).
options.B: A passive question asking whether two things are identical.
options.C: A mathematical multiplication operator.

questions.prompt: What operator must you use in Class 7.1 if you want to ask the Boolean question 'Are these two things identical?'

options.A: A double equals sign (`==`) to evaluate equality.
options.B: A single equals sign (`=`).
options.C: A semicolon (`;`).

questions.prompt: Why does Class 7.1 instruct you to force your eyes to read variable assignments from right to left?

options.A: Because you must figure out the final resulting value on the right side of `=` first before placing it into the variable bucket waiting on the left.
options.B: Because computer monitors display text upside down.
options.C: Because Boolean gates only read comments.

questions.prompt: In Section 5 of Class 7.1, what are 'hat chains'?

options.A: Small modular contract blocks that snap together to form dependencies where breaking a prerequisite automatically revokes downstream access.
options.B: Physical paper folders stored in a law library.
options.C: Email threads between opposing counsel.

questions.prompt: In Class 7.1's subscription example of hat chains, what happens if a patron stops paying their subscription?

options.A: The prerequisite contract breaks and their downstream 'reader hat' access is automatically revoked by the runtime without human enforcement.
options.B: Nothing happens until a paralegal audits the account a year later.
options.C: The patron is granted permanent administrator privileges.

questions.prompt: In Class 7.1's transportation metaphor, what do the Horse-and-Buggy, the Car, and the Waymo represent?

options.A: Direct law (manual drafting), Mechanized law (coding smart contracts with human drivers), and Automated law (fully autonomous self-executing systems).
options.B: Three types of municipal traffic tickets.
options.C: Three generations of paper printing presses.

questions.prompt: What governs asset transfers and legal relationships inside the 'Waymo' stage of Automated Law?

options.A: Strict true and false Boolean gates executing autonomously at runtime.
options.B: Manual paper filing clerks stamping physical forms.
options.C: Ambiguous 'and/or' clauses interpreted by juries.

questions.prompt: What is the 'engineering path' in the two diverging career paths described at the end of Class 7.1?

options.A: Developers acting like modern patent agents — specialized legal authorities who write the complex under-the-hood computational logic.
options.B: Traditional litigators who refuse to use computers.
options.C: Court stenographers transcribing hearings by hand.

questions.prompt: What is the 'lawyering path' described at the end of Class 7.1?

options.A: Traditional lawyers who evolve to write their daily legal deliverables using programming syntax as society transitions from static sheets to active scripts.
options.B: Abandoning legal practice to become mechanical automotive engineers.
options.C: Drafting exclusively on parchment with quill pens.
